analysis.one_liner: Creates a government office to manufacture and sell cheap generic drugs like insulin directly.
analysis.headline: The bill to have the government manufacture affordable generic drugs, including insulin, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Drug Manufacturing Act would create an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services. That office would make and sell generic versions of drugs where only a few companies control the market and prices are high or supplies run short, starting with every type of insulin, asthma inhalers, EpiPens, overdose-reversal naloxone, and key antibiotics. It would sell them at a 'fair price' based on manufacturing cost and patient access, publish all its prices, and bar former drug-industry lobbyists and executives of companies under federal enforcement from running or working in the office.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay high out-of-pocket prices for drugs in markets with few competitors: people who use insulin, asthma and COPD inhalers, epinephrine auto-injectors, and naloxone; federal, state, and local health programs that buy these drugs; and taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid. Patients facing shortages of essential medicines would also benefit from a reliable public manufacturer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients priced out of insulin and other generics

how_it_helps.text: Requires the new office to begin public manufacturing of at least one insulin product of each dosage form and type, plus an inhaler, an epinephrine auto-injector, naloxone, and at least three antibiotics within one year of enactment.

Requires the office to sell drugs at a 'fair price' that accounts for patient access, manufacturing cost, and the cost to federal and state health programs, and to publish all prices it pays and charges.

Targets drugs with three or fewer manufacturers that have raised prices above inflation, are in shortage, or are priced so high that patients cannot access them — the markets where patients currently face the least competition.
Bars former registered drug-industry lobbyists, and senior executives of drug companies under federal enforcement actions, from running or working in the office for six years after leaving industry.

Allows the office to sell its FDA-approved applications to other manufacturers after three years, revoking the sale and resuming production if the buyer fails to market the drug or raises its price above the fair price plus inflation.

analysis.who_pays: The brand-name and generic drug companies whose markets are targeted — they would face a well-funded public competitor selling at cost-based prices. Taxpayers would also fund the office's startup, since the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' with no offset, though the office's own drug sales would later fund its operations.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes unlimited new appropriations with no offset, so taxpayers would fund building federal drug manufacturing capacity up front; the office only becomes self-funding later through drug sales.

The government entering the generic drug business is a major expansion of federal activity, and critics argue private manufacturers could be discouraged from investing in markets where they might now compete with a government producer that can sell at cost.

Requiring the office to manufacture roughly 15 drugs within a year and 25 within three years is an aggressive timeline for FDA approvals and building manufacturing, and failure would undercut the program's credibility.

The bill's scope is narrower than the drug price problem: it only applies to drugs with expired patents and exclusivities, so it would not touch brand-name drugs still under patent, which are the biggest cost driver for many patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who use insulin, inhalers, epinephrine, or naloxone, the potential benefit is large and direct: a public manufacturer selling these essentials at cost-based prices where only a few private sellers exist. The real costs are taxpayer-funded startup spending and an unproven track record — no government has run a generic drug business at this scale — but the bill's transparency requirements, lobbyist bans, and requirement that the FDA treat its applications like any other company's are designed to guard against the most obvious failures. The bill never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be publicly weighed in a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on December 5, 2023, with nine other Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced.
Three days later it was referred to the committee's Health Subcommittee.
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers are better off: no public competitor was created, and existing insulin, inhaler, and epinephrine prices were untouched. Officeholders who preferred not to act on drug manufacturing also avoided the issue.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Affordable Drug Manufacturing Act of 2023 in the House.

for.name: Reps. Barbara Lee, Jonathan Jackson, Eleanor Holmes Norton, Pramila Jayapal, Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, Danny Davis, Jesús García, Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors; ten Democrats cosponsored the bill in total, all from one party.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the House majority party
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the entire two-year Congress, leaving it to die in subcommittee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Set the chamber's agenda; controlled which bills reached the floor
against.what_they_did: Bills that clear committee but are not scheduled by leadership cannot get a floor vote; with Republican control of the House in the 118th Congress, a bill with only Democratic sponsorship had no path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support, and the bill was referred to a Republican-run committee that took no action on it.

industries.note: A government office selling insulin, inhalers, epinephrine auto-injectors, naloxone, and antibiotics at cost-based prices would compete directly with the few companies that dominate those markets. Prices those companies charge patients and public health programs would face downward pressure for the first time.

industries.industry: Drug wholesalers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The office would sell to wholesalers and direct purchasers at a published fair price, and the advisory council would include wholesalers, pharmacies, and PBMs — so intermediaries keep their role in distribution. But published prices reduce the opacity these intermediaries currently benefit from.
The bill directs the office to contract for manufacturing with a preference for nonprofit entities and public partners, creating a new customer and revenue source for public-interest drug producers.
